In 'An Iridescence on the Water', what is the primary Dhamma theme and practical guidance offered?

In 'An Iridescence on the Water', the teaching opens with this observation: *"Translator's note: Chao Khun Nararatana, prior to his ordination, was a member of King Rama VI's personal staff, and was so trusted by the king that he was given the rank of chao phraya — the highest Thai rank of conferred nobility — when he was only 25."* The central invitation is to turn one's investigation inward — to verify the Dhamma not as an external philosophy, but as directly observable reality in one's own body, speech, and mind. As the text emphasizes, the Dhamma is *akāliko* (timeless) and *opanayiko* (leading inward), realizable (*paccattaṁ*) by each practitioner through patient, honest awareness.

In 'An Iridescence on the Water', what does the section on '§1. Personal Magnetism' teach regarding spiritual practice?

In the section '§1. Personal Magnetism', the text points out: *"To receive the sympathy and compassion of others depends on a combination of our own good qualities, such as energy, industry, perseverance, strength, resilience, together with a heart of sympathy and compassion toward others, without conceit or pride...."* This part of the teaching instructs the meditator to look closely at the underlying movements of the mind rather than getting lost in superficial reactions. By maintaining steady, unattached mindfulness, we allow mental formations (*saṅkhāras*) to arise, reveal their impermanent nature, and cease without grasping or resistance. This direct seeing is the true doorway to peace.

How does 'An Iridescence on the Water' explain the role of anicca (impermanence (anicca)) in meditation?

In 'An Iridescence on the Water', anicca is discussed in this context: *"He taught us to put our views at peace through discernment, reflecting so as to see that:
All things are undependable and inconstant (aniccam)."* Here, anicca (impermanence (anicca) — all conditioned phenomena arise and pass away) is treated not as a theoretical doctrine, but as a living faculty to be actively cultivated and observed. When we bring genuine mindfulness to our direct experience, the quality of anicca helps dismantle habitual delusion and stabilizes the mind in clear, unentangled awareness.

In 'An Iridescence on the Water', anattā is discussed in this context: *"(Thus they are said to be anatta or not-self.)
When we see these truths, the mind becomes strong, resilient, stable, and resolute, unaffected by events — because we have seen the truth, with our own discernment, that such things are undependable and unstable; that they have to change, deteriorate, and disband; that they don't lie under our power."* Here, anattā (not-self (anattā)) is treated not as a theoretical doctrine, but as a living faculty to be actively cultivated and observed.
